newsitem.title: USA: Newmont raises bid for Santa Fe Pacific to $2.2 billion.
newsitem.headline: Newmont raises bid for Santa Fe Pacific to $2.2 billion.

text.p: Newmont Mining Corp. Tuesday raised its hostile takeover bid for Santa Fe Pacific Gold Corp. to $2.2 billion in stock in an attempt to derail the company's proposed merger with Homestake Mining Co.

Santa Fe agreed on Dec. 9 to be acquired by Homestake in a stock deal then valued at $17.42 a share, or $2.3 billion. But Homestake's bid of 1.115 of its shares for each Santa Fe share is now worth only about $15.05 a share, or $2 billion.
Denver-based Newmont said it was offering 0.40 share of its stock, worth $16.50, for each of Santa Fe's 133 million shares, well above its initial offer of 0.33 of a share made on Dec. 5.
Newmont also said it asked Santa Fe to enter talks aimed at terminating Santa Fe's merger agreement with Homestake.
"The combination of our two companies is the best fit at the best price with unparalleled opportunities to create long-term value," Newmont Chairman Ronald Cambre said.
He said one key reason Santa Fe shareholders should support Newmont's bid was its low cost of production, which is especially important given the recent fall in gold prices.
In the last month or so, the stocks of gold mining companies have dropped, mirroring a decline of almost $9 an ounce, to under $360, in the price of gold.
Cambre said Newmont's cash cost of producing gold, about $202 an ounce, would rise to about $215 if it merged with Santa Fe, which he called equal to Santa Fe's current cost of production.
If the Homestake merger goes through, he said shareholders would face higher production costs since Homestake's cash cost was $248 an ounce.
San Francisco-based Homestake said it planned to complete its merger with Santa Fe Pacific Gold, based in Albuquerque, N.M.

"We fully intend to complete our planned transaction, which effectively gives Santa Fe's shareholders about 50 percent of the combined company and which we believe offers much greater upside potential than Newmont's offer," Homestake Chief Executive Officer Jack Thompson said.
Newmont also said it was filing materials with the Securities and Exchange Commission and planned to start its hostile tender offer when it received regulatory approval.

The offer is subject to the exchange of at least 90 percent of Santa Fe's common shares, the ability to merge with Santa Fe on a pooling of interests basis, and the withdrawal of Santa Fe's takeover defence plan.
Newmont said that at the current gold price the merger would boost reserves immediately, increase earnings in the year after the deal closes and raise production and cash flow in the second year.
Newmont Mining owns 91 percent of Newmont Gold Co., a leading global gold producer with operations in Nevada, Peru, Uzbekistan and Indonesia.
Santa Fe Pacific Gold owns mines in Nevada and California.
Homestake has major mining properties in the United States, Canada and Australia and is exploring for gold in the Andes, Venezuela, French Guiana, Brazil and other areas.
Santa Fe stock rose 87.5 cents to $15.125, Newmont fell 75 cents to $40.50 and Homestake added 56.25 cents to $13.69, all on the New York Stock Exchange.
